\chapter{Telling Somebody To Do Something}
\label{ch:hi-adesh}
\hlchaptermodality{93}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can give a command at the right level of politeness, say you are at the familiar level, tell somebody not to do something, and read the negative notices a public sign is made of.}

Read a public notice and say the same thing as a friend would say it, noticing that a sign is at the aap level because it addresses a stranger.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bolo]{\hi{बोलो} — a command at the level you already know how to choose}

\label{lesson:HI-C85-bolo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{tumhārā}. You learned that Hindi has three levels of \emph{you} and that the possessive changes with each. Say the verb \emph{bolnā}. This chapter does the same thing to the verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बोलो}}
\textbf{\hi{बोलो}} (\emph{bolo}) — \textquotedblleft{}speak,\textquotedblright{} said to somebody you would call \textbf{\hi{तुम}}.

Take the verb, drop the \textbf{-\hi{ना}}, add \textbf{-o}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{bolnā} $\to$ \textbf{bol} $\to$ \textbf{bolo}
\end{quote}

The same operation on any verb: \emph{karnā} $\to$ \emph{karo}, \emph{sunnā} $\to$ \emph{suno}, \emph{calnā} $\to$ \emph{calo}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the command carries the level, and nothing else has to}]
This is the part that makes the imperative economical. In English a command is one word for everybody — \emph{speak} — and politeness has to be added around it: \emph{speak}, \emph{please speak}, \emph{would you mind speaking}.

In Hindi the \textbf{verb ending itself} carries the level:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{level} & \textbf{the form} & \textbf{to whom} \\
\midrule
\hi{तुम} & \textbf{\hi{बोलो}} & a friend, a sibling \\
\hi{आप} & boliye & a stranger, an elder \\
\hi{तू} & bol & intimate, or rude \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You already know how to choose between those three, because you chose between \emph{tumhārā}, \emph{āpkā} and \emph{terā} the same way. The pronoun does not even have to be said: \textbf{\hi{बोलो}} on its own tells the listener which one you meant.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बोलो}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{bolo}, speak
  \item the two steps that build it from \emph{bolnā}
  \item \emph{suno} and \emph{karo}, built the same way
  \item who you would say \emph{bolo} to, and who you would not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How is \emph{bolo} built from \emph{bolnā}? (Drop the \textbf{-\hi{ना}}, add \textbf{-o}.) Which of the three \emph{you}s does it belong to? (\emph{Tum}.) Does the pronoun have to be spoken? (No — the ending says it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[boliye]{\hi{बोलिए} — the ending you have been saying for eighty chapters}

\label{lesson:HI-C85-boliye}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{māf kījiye}. You learned it as one lump meaning \textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{} Say it again and listen to the end of the second word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बोलिए}}
\textbf{\hi{बोलिए}} (\emph{boliye}) — \textquotedblleft{}please speak,\textquotedblright{} said to somebody you would call \textbf{\hi{आप}}.

The ending is \textbf{-iye}, on the same stem as before:

\begin{quote}
\emph{bolnā} $\to$ \textbf{bol} $\to$ \textbf{boliye}
\end{quote}

And now the lump comes apart. \textbf{\hi{कीजिए}} is \emph{karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to do,\textquotedblright{} with this same ending: \emph{kar} + \emph{-iye}. \emph{Māf kījiye} is literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}please do forgiveness.\textquotedblright{}} You have been giving a respectful command since the ninth chapter without knowing it was one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: politeness is built in, not added on}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{command} & \textbf{how politeness is carried} \\
\midrule
English & speak & by adding \emph{please} \\
Hindi \hi{तुम} & \hi{बोलो} & by the ending \\
Hindi \hi{आप} & \hi{बोलिए} & by the ending \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{बोलिए}} already contains the respect, so it needs no \emph{kṛpayā}. Adding one is not wrong — it is warmer, the way \emph{would you mind} is warmer than \emph{please} — but the bare form is complete and polite on its own.

A stem ending in a vowel lengthens slightly before \textbf{-iye}: \emph{karnā} gives \textbf{kījiye}, not \emph{kariye}, and \emph{denā} gives \textbf{dījiye}. Those two are the ones you will meet most, and you already had the first.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बोलिए}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{boliye}, please speak
  \item \emph{bolo} and \emph{boliye} one after the other, and name who each is for
  \item what \emph{māf kījiye} literally asks for (please do forgiveness)
  \item whether \emph{boliye} needs \emph{kṛpayā} in front of it (no)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending makes the respectful command? (\textbf{-iye}.) What verb is hiding inside \emph{kījiye}? (\emph{Karnā}, to do.) Which of \emph{bolo} and \emph{boliye} would you use with a stranger? (\emph{Boliye}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tum ho]{\hi{तुम} \hi{हो} — the copula that was hiding inside one question}

\label{lesson:HI-C85-tum-ho}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{tumhārā}. You can name the \emph{tum} level and command at it. Say \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{} at that level, and notice you have never been given the word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{तुम} \hi{हो}}
\textbf{\hi{तुम} \hi{हो}} (\emph{tum ho}) — \textquotedblleft{}you are,\textquotedblright{} at the \emph{tum} level.

\textbf{\hi{हो}} is the copula that goes with \textbf{\hi{तुम}}, and nothing else takes it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the copula, completed}]
You have had the others for a long time. Here they are together, which is the first time the set has been complete:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{subject} & \textbf{copula} \\
\midrule
\hi{मैं} & \hi{हूँ} \\
\hi{तुम} & \textbf{\hi{हो}} \\
\hi{आप} & \hi{हैं} \\
\hi{वह} & \hi{है} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four forms and no irregularity beyond having to learn them. \textbf{\hi{हो}} is the one that was missing, and it was missing in an awkward way: the track has been saying it inside the age question all along, as a lump, without the form ever standing on its own.

Now it can. \emph{Tum acchhe ho}, \emph{tum śarmīle ho} — any of the character adjectives you have, at the familiar level.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: matching the level all the way through}]
A sentence has to keep one level from end to end:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{level} & \textbf{copula} & \textbf{command} \\
\midrule
\hi{तुम} & \textbf{\hi{हो}} & \hi{बोलो} \\
\hi{आप} & \hi{हैं} & \hi{बोलिए} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Mixing them — \emph{āp ho}, or \emph{tum boliye} — is the error a listener notices at once, in the way an English speaker notices \emph{you was}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four copula forms with their subjects
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{तुम} \hi{हो}\textquotedblright{}, and then the same meaning at the \emph{āp} level
  \item a sentence describing a friend, keeping the \emph{tum} level throughout
  \item why \emph{āp ho} sounds wrong
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which subject takes \textbf{\hi{हो}}? (\emph{Tum}, and only \emph{tum}.) What goes wrong in \emph{tum boliye}? (The pronoun is at one level and the verb at another.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mat]{\hi{मत} — the word Hindi keeps for saying \textquotedblleft{}don't\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C85-mat}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{bolo} and \emph{boliye}. Now say the opposite of each — and notice that the negative you already know is not the one Hindi uses here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मत}}
\textbf{\hi{मत}} (\emph{mat}) — \textquotedblleft{}don't,\textquotedblright{} and it goes \textbf{in front of the verb}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मत} \hi{बोलिए}} — \emph{mat boliye} — please don't speak. \textbf{\hi{मत} \hi{बोलो}} — \emph{mat bolo} — don't speak.
\end{quote}

Hindi has a negative for statements, which you already have, and a \textbf{separate one reserved for commands}. Using the statement negative to tell somebody not to do something is the mistake an English speaker makes, because English uses \emph{not} for both.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the sign you will actually meet it on}]
A negative command is what a public notice \textbf{is}. This is the shape:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{notice} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\hi{यहाँ} \hi{मत} \hi{बैठिए} & please do not sit here \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three pieces, and you have all three: \emph{yahā̃} here, \emph{mat} don't, \emph{baiṭhiye} the respectful command from \emph{baiṭhnā}, built with the ending from the last lesson.

Notice the politeness level. A public sign addresses a stranger, so it uses the \textbf{\hi{आप}} form — which is why a reading paper's notices are full of \textbf{-iye} and why that ending was worth taking apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मत} \hi{बोलो}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मत} \hi{बोलिए}\textquotedblright{}, and name who each is for
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{यहाँ} \hi{मत} \hi{बैठिए}\textquotedblright{}, and take it apart into its three pieces
  \item where \emph{mat} stands relative to the verb (in front)
  \item why a public sign uses the \textbf{-iye} form
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which negative does Hindi keep for commands? (\textbf{\hi{मत}}.) Where does it stand? (In front of the verb.) Why do public notices use the respectful ending? (A sign addresses a stranger.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tīn star, ek kriyā]{tīn star, ek kriyā — three levels running through everything}

\label{lesson:HI-C85-repaso-adesh}



\begin{quote}
Say the command for \textquotedblleft{}speak\textquotedblright{} at both levels you can now use, and name who each one is for.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same choice, made four times}]
The level is not a fact about the verb. It is a fact about \textbf{who you are talking to}, and every part of the sentence agrees to it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{level} & \textbf{possessive} & \textbf{copula} \\
\midrule
\hi{तू} & \hi{तेरा} & \hi{है} \\
\hi{तुम} & \hi{तुम्हारा} & \textbf{\hi{हो}} \\
\hi{आप} & \hi{आपका} & \hi{हैं} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{level} & \textbf{command} & \textbf{negative command} \\
\midrule
\hi{तू} & \hi{बोल} & \hi{मत} \hi{बोल} \\
\hi{तुम} & \textbf{\hi{बोलो}} & \hi{मत} \hi{बोलो} \\
\hi{आप} & \textbf{\hi{बोलिए}} & \hi{मत} \hi{बोलिए} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read each row straight across. Choosing a person picks the whole row, and every cell in it follows. That is the saving: one decision, not four.

The \textbf{\hi{तू}} row is there for recognition. A learner should read it and not produce it — it is intimate between close friends and insulting to anyone else, and the risk of getting it wrong is much larger than the benefit of using it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: how each command is built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{level} & \textbf{from \emph{bolnā}} & \textbf{ending} \\
\midrule
\hi{तू} & \hi{बोल} & the bare stem \\
\hi{तुम} & \hi{बोलो} & \textbf{-o} \\
\hi{आप} & \hi{बोलिए} & \textbf{-iye} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three endings, one stem. And as the table above showed, \textbf{\hi{मत}} is the same word at every level — the negative does not change with politeness, only the verb does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the \emph{tum} row straight across — possessive, copula, command
  \item the \emph{āp} row the same way
  \item \emph{suno} and \emph{suniye}, built from \emph{sunnā} with the two endings
  \item the negative of each command you have made
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does choosing a level of \emph{you} decide? (A whole row — possessive, copula and command together.) Which row should a learner read but not use? (\textbf{\hi{तू}}.) Does the negative change with the level? (No — \emph{mat} is the same at all three.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yahā̃ mat baiṭhiye]{\hi{यहाँ} \hi{मत} \hi{बैठिए} — a notice is the whole chapter in three words}

\label{lesson:HI-C85-sintesis-suchna}



\begin{quote}
Say the negative command word and the respectful ending. A public sign is made of nothing else.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why a notice is always at the aap level}]
A sign does not know who is reading it, so it addresses a stranger — and a stranger takes \textbf{\hi{आप}}. That single fact explains the shape of almost every notice a reading paper prints:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{on the sign} & \textbf{at the tum level it would be} \\
\midrule
\hi{यहाँ} \hi{मत} \hi{बैठिए} & \hi{यहाँ} \hi{मत} \hi{बैठो} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The second is what a friend says to you. The first is what a wall says to everybody, which is why \textbf{-iye} is worth more to a reader than \textbf{-o}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read these aloud. Every word has been taught:

\begin{quote}
\hi{यहाँ} \hi{मत} \hi{बैठिए।} \hi{यहाँ} \hi{मत} \hi{बोलिए।} \hi{कृपया} \hi{सुनिए।}
\end{quote}

Three notices, and the pattern is identical in all three: the respectful ending, with \emph{mat} in front when the notice forbids and nothing in front when it asks.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{यहाँ} \hi{मत} \hi{बैठिए}\textquotedblright{}, and translate it
  \item the same notice as a friend would say it to you
  \item a notice telling people not to speak
  \item why a sign uses \emph{āp} rather than \emph{tum}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{तुम} \hi{हो}\textquotedblright{}, and say which of the two notices above matches that level
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is a public notice at the \emph{āp} level? (It addresses a stranger.) What turns an asking notice into a forbidding one? (\emph{Mat}, in front of the verb.)
\end{tcolorbox}
